title: CPU caches, false sharing and @Contended
goal: By the end you can explain why two threads writing different fields can slow each other down, check field offsets with JOL, pad hot fields apart, and know when `LongAdder` is the better answer.
opening:
Picture two cooks at one counter, sharing a single cutting board. One chops onions, the other chops peppers. They never touch each other's vegetables, so there's nothing to argue about. But only one knife fits on the board at a time, so each cook keeps stepping back to wait for the other.

Your processor has the same problem in miniature. Two threads, two lines of work running at the same time, can slow each other down even when each writes only its own field. The two fields share one small block of memory, and the hardware moves that block around as a unit.

It's an easy trap, because the code looks perfect: no shared data, no locks, no race. And this time the JIT isn't involved at all; the cost lives in the hardware. Lesson 3 gave us honest benchmarks on one thread; now a second thread joins. In this lesson, we'll see how caches move memory, read real field offsets, set two counters fighting over one line, pad them apart, and meet the JDK's own answer, `LongAdder`. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: In the report service, one thread only ever writes `stats.parsed` (documents parsed), and another only ever writes `stats.written` (reports written). Both fields are `volatile long` in the same small object. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing: they never touch the same field, so there's no contention
Lost updates, because `++` on a volatile isn't atomic
Both threads can slow down, because the two fields share a cache line that the cores keep taking from each other
A deadlock between the two threads
warmup.why: Caches move memory in 64-byte lines, and a core that writes a line needs the only copy. Two fields 8 bytes apart sit on one line, so every write by one thread invalidates the other core's copy, and the other way round. Nothing is lost: each field has a single writer, so `++` on it is safe. How much time it costs depends on the machine, as the section on false sharing shows.

sections.h: False sharing: two threads, two fields, one line
sections.body:
The parsing thread now writes only `parsed`, and the writing thread writes only `written`. They share no data, so there's nothing to lock and no race, no two threads writing the same variable. But they share a line, and the line can live in only one core's cache for writing at a time.

Trace two writes. Core 1 holds the line and adds 1 to `parsed`. Core 2 wants to add 1 to `written`, finds its copy invalid, and waits while the line travels over. Now core 1's copy is invalid, so its next `parsed++` waits for the line to travel back. Each `++` is a few nanoseconds of work wrapped in a wait. When both threads run at the same moment, the line bounces between the cores on almost every write. This is **false sharing**: the program shares nothing, and the hardware shares a lot. The figure shows the bounce.

`FalseSharingDemo` runs exactly that, 25 million increments per thread: first with the adjacent fields, then with the fields padded apart. Before you read on, decide what you expect. Here is one run on the busy course machine:

```text
round 1: adjacent   994 ms   padded   785 ms
round 2: adjacent   977 ms   padded   784 ms
round 3: adjacent 1,124 ms   padded   806 ms
```

That's a gap, but a small one, and it wasn't even steady. Across nine runs here, in Java and Kotlin, the padded version lost one round in three. Was the mechanism wrong? No. More than 20 other busy programs were sharing the machine's four cores, so our two threads were rarely running at the same moment. A line can only bounce between two cores that both want it right now. When this lesson was first written, on a quieter day, the same demo on the same machine told the textbook story: adjacent took 957 to 1,387 ms and padded 206 to 247 ms, about five times faster.

Where the threads run matters too. Two hyperthreads, two hardware threads that share one physical core, also share that core's L1 and L2 caches. Put the two writers there, and there's no line to bounce at all.

So don't promise anyone a speed-up from padding. The mechanism is certain, and the size of the effect isn't. The only way to know is to measure on the hardware you run on, under the load you run with. When it does hit, it hits code that looks perfectly innocent: a stats object with one counter per worker thread, or an array of per-thread totals whose slots sit 8 bytes apart.

**Separate fields aren't separate memory. Fields that different threads write in a hot loop need lines of their own.**

The cure, when you need it, is space between the fields. Java makes that a little harder than it sounds.

try.title: Race two counters on one line
steps: Read `FalseSharingDemo`. Predict: will the adjacent run be slower, the same, or faster than the padded one on your machine?
Close other busy programs if you can. Run it, then run it again. Then run the Kotlin twin.
If you see a big gap, check how many physical cores your machine has (`lscpu` on Linux, `sysctl -n hw.physicalcpu` on macOS). If you see none, check how busy the machine is (`uptime` shows the load).

On a busy machine it can lose, as it did on the course machine (about 690 ms against 1,150 ms). With one thread, the counts are 10,000,000 and `AtomicLong` wins: 103 ms against 181 ms in the last round on the course machine. With no contention, `LongAdder` only touches its base field, its cells never exist, and its extra checks are pure cost.

compare.title: A padded counter in Java and Kotlin

java.title: StageCounters.java

kotlin.title: StageCounters.kt

compare.note: Both compile to the same JVM classes with the same field layout, because the JVM decides the layout, not the language. The differences are in what you write. Kotlin classes are final by default, so the padding classes need `abstract` or `open`. A Kotlin `var` property is a private field plus a getter and a setter; `@JvmField` exposes the field directly, and `@Volatile` makes it volatile. In both languages the padding fields are never read, and nothing in either language promises the order of fields within one class, which is why the chain of classes is the safer trick.

worked.title: Find false sharing in a stats object and fix it

steps.say: The report service has two worker threads, and each updates its own counter in one shared stats object. A profile shows both threads spending time in `record`, which does almost nothing. Start by printing the layout.
The two hot fields are 8 bytes apart. Worker 0 writes `done0`, worker 1 writes `done1`, and both sit on one line. This is JOL's real output on JDK 25.
steps.code:
OFF  SZ   TYPE DESCRIPTION               VALUE
  0   8        (object header: mark)     N/A
  8   4        (object header: class)    N/A
 12   4        (alignment/padding gap)   
 16   8   long WorkerStats.done0         N/A
 24   8   long WorkerStats.done1         N/A
Instance size: 32 bytes

steps.say: Give each worker its own object instead of padding one. Two `WorkerCounter` objects created one after the other can still end up next to each other in memory, so if the profile still shows the problem, pad the counter class or use a `LongAdder`. Self-check: why don't separate objects guarantee separate lines? (Answer: each thread gets new objects from its own stretch of the heap, one after another, so two small objects created together are often only a few bytes apart.)

Verify with a forked JMH benchmark that runs two threads, on the hardware and under the load you deploy to, not on your laptop alone. Keep the version that measures faster there. If neither is clearly faster, keep the simpler code.

lab.title: Pad two counters and fix a metrics counter
steps: Open `StageCounters`, the report service's two counters: `parsed`, written only by the parsing thread, and `written`, written only by the writing thread. Then open `RequestMetrics`, which every request thread calls once per report. Run the tests. Three of four fail: `parsed` and `written` are 8 bytes apart (at 16 and 24), and `RequestMetrics` loses updates when 8 threads record at once.

Lay out `StageCounters` so `parsed` and `written` are at least 64 bytes apart. Keep both fields `volatile long` with those exact names, and keep the public methods. A chain of classes is the reliable way.
Fix `RequestMetrics` so `count()` and `totalWords()` are exact under contention. Writes happen on every request and reads every few seconds, so pick the tool built for that.
Run the tests until all four pass. Run them twice: the metrics tests are race tests.
Optional: print `ClassLayout.parseClass(StageCounters.class).toPrintable()` in a scratch test and look at your layout.
hints: HotSpot lays out superclass fields before subclass fields. `abstract class ParsedCounter { volatile long parsed; }`, then a class with eight `long` padding fields extending it, then a class with `written` extending that, and `StageCounters` at the end of the chain.
The fields in the superclasses can't be `private` if `StageCounters` needs to read them. Package-private works, and JOL finds fields in superclasses too.

`count++` on a `volatile` is a read and a write, so two threads can both read 41 and both write 42. With many writers, `LongAdder.increment()` and `add(words)` are exact and spread the writes over padded cells.
The reference solution puts `written` 72 bytes after `parsed` and passes on JDK 21 and JDK 25.
lab.done_when: All four tests in `CacheLineTest` pass, twice in a row.

drill.title: Explain a layout and write the fix from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. JOL prints `parsed` at offset 16 and `written` at offset 24 for a class that two threads write. Write two sentences on what goes wrong and why, then write a padded version using a chain of classes. Then write the one-line answer you'd give for a request counter written by 200 threads.

recap: Caches move memory in 64-byte lines, and a core that writes a line invalidates every other core's copy.

False sharing: two threads writing different fields on the same line make it bounce between cores. It costs time, never correctness, and how much depends on the hardware and on whether the threads really run at once.

Pad hot fields at least 64 bytes apart. A chain of classes is reliable; padding fields in one class may be reordered; `@Contended` needs `-XX:-RestrictContended` and an internal export for your own classes.
Check layouts with JOL and assert distances, not offsets: headers differ between JDKs and flags (compact object headers are the default in JDK 27).
For counters in your own code, use `LongAdder`: its cells are padded with `@Contended` and only created under contention. Without contention, `AtomicLong` is a little faster.
The limit: everything here makes one known hot spot cheaper. None of it tells you where a running program actually spends its time; that's what the profilers in the next lessons are for.
closing:
We started with two cooks who never touch each other's vegetables and still keep waiting, because they share one cutting board. Two threads that write two fields on one cache line do the same, and padding, a chain of classes or `LongAdder`'s padded cells give each its own board. How much it costs depends on the machine, so measure where you run.

Now look in your code for an array or object where each thread writes its own slot or field in a busy loop. Slots 8 bytes apart share a line.

Next, we'll stop guessing where a running program spends its time: how can the JDK Flight Recorder log what the JVM was doing, on one clock, cheaply enough to leave on?

quiz.q: JOL shows `w0` at offset 16 and `w1` at offset 24 in a stats object. Thread 0 only writes `w0`, thread 1 only writes `w1`. What is the problem, if any?
options: A race: updates to `w0` and `w1` can be lost
False sharing: the fields share a cache line, so the two cores keep invalidating each other's copy
None: different fields never interact
The object is too big to fit in a cache line
quiz.why: 8 bytes apart means one 64-byte line. Each field has one writer, so nothing is lost, but every write takes the line away from the other core. That costs time, not correctness.

quiz.q: You annotate two fields of your own class with `@jdk.internal.vm.annotation.Contended`, compile it, and run it normally. JOL shows them at 16 and 24. Why?
options: `@Contended` only works on JDK 27
JOL can't see padding
The JVM ignores `@Contended` outside the JDK unless you run with `-XX:-RestrictContended`
The fields must also be `final`
quiz.why: `RestrictContended` is true by default, so the annotation only takes effect in JDK classes. With `-XX:-RestrictContended`, the same class shows the fields at 144 and 280. The JVM prints no warning either way.

quiz.q: A metrics counter is incremented by every request thread and read by a monitoring program every 10 seconds. Which is the best fit?
options: A `volatile long` with `count++`
An `AtomicLong`
A `long` field inside a `synchronized` method
A `LongAdder`
quiz.why: Many writers and rare reads is exactly what `LongAdder` is for: under contention, each thread mostly updates its own padded cell. `AtomicLong` is correct but makes all writers fight over one line. `volatile` with `++` loses updates.

quiz.q: Your test checks that two fields are "at offset 16 and offset 88". It passes on JDK 21 and fails on JDK 27. What's the best fix?
options: Assert the distance between the fields (at least 64 bytes) instead of absolute offsets
Pin the tests to JDK 21
Turn off JOL on JDK 27
Add more padding until both pass
quiz.why: JDK 27 turns compact object headers on by default, so every field moves by a few bytes. The distance between the two fields is what decides whether they share a line, and it doesn't depend on the header size.

quiz.q: From the first track: two threads call `counter.incrementAndGet()` on a shared `AtomicLong` 10 million times each. Then you switch to `LongAdder.increment()`. What changes in the result?
options: `LongAdder` may lose some increments, but it's faster
Nothing: both count exactly. Under real contention `LongAdder` usually gets there faster
`AtomicLong` loses increments under contention
`LongAdder.sum()` is always more up to date than `AtomicLong.get()`
quiz.why: Both are exact once all the writes finish. `LongAdder` spreads writes over cells so threads stop fighting over one cache line, which pays off when they really run at the same time. Its `sum()` is not an atomic snapshot while writes are still happening, which is why decisions should use `AtomicLong`.

flashcards.front: How big is a cache line on x86?
flashcards.back: 64 bytes. Caches move whole lines, never single fields.
Threads writing different fields that sit on the same cache line, so the line keeps moving between cores. It costs time, not correctness.

flashcards.front: How far apart must two hot fields be to avoid sharing a 64-byte line?
flashcards.back: At least 64 bytes between their offsets.

flashcards.front: Why is a chain of classes better than padding fields inside one class?
flashcards.back: HotSpot lays out superclass fields before subclass fields; within one class the JVM may reorder fields, even of the same type.

flashcards.front: What does `@Contended` need to work on your own classes?
flashcards.back: `-XX:-RestrictContended` at run time (otherwise it's silently ignored) and `--add-exports java.base/jdk.internal.vm.annotation=ALL-UNNAMED` to compile.
Under contention it spreads updates over `Striped64.Cell` objects, each padded with `@Contended` (JOL shows the value at offset 144). `sum()` adds them up.

flashcards.front: Why should a layout test assert distances, not offsets?
flashcards.back: Header sizes differ between JDKs and flags: compact object headers (default in JDK 27) move every field.

terms.plain: The unit a CPU cache moves around: 64 bytes on x86.
The hardware keeping every core's copy of a line consistent, by invalidating copies on writes.
Different data on one cache line, written by different cores, making the line bounce between them.
Unused bytes placed between fields so they land on different cache lines.
A JDK-internal annotation that makes the JVM pad a field or class, 128 bytes by default.
Java Object Layout, a tool that prints the real field offsets and object sizes.
A counter that spreads contended updates over padded cells and adds them up on read.

explain_back.prompt: Explain to a teammate why giving each worker thread its own field in a shared stats object didn't make the counters fast, and what you'd do instead.
explain_back.answer: The fields are separate, so there's no race, but they sit 8 bytes apart, which puts them on the same 64-byte cache line. A core can only write a line it holds alone, so each write by one thread invalidates the other core's copy, and the line moves back and forth on almost every update. That's false sharing. One fix is to pad the fields at least 64 bytes apart, ideally with a chain of classes because the JVM may reorder fields within one class, and to check the offsets with JOL. For ordinary counters I'd use a LongAdder per counter instead: it creates padded cells only when threads contend and adds them up when we read. And I'd only believe a speed-up after measuring it on our real hardware under real load, because how much false sharing costs depends on the CPU and on whether the threads truly run at the same time.

deeper.body:
JMH protects you from one source of false sharing automatically. Its false-sharing sample says "@States are automatically padded", but "This padding does not extend to the State internals". Fields inside your `@State` object can still share a line, which is exactly what that sample demonstrates, with several fixes side by side. To measure it on your own hardware, run that sample with several forks on a machine with real cores and little else running.

Why does the JDK pad with 128 bytes when lines are 64? The flag `ContendedPaddingWidth` only says how many bytes to pad. A common explanation is that some processors also fetch the neighbouring line, so a 64-byte gap can still let two hot fields interfere. This course couldn't check that against a primary source, so treat 128 as "the JDK's safe default" rather than a rule.

Two other tools look at the same problem from the hardware side. `perf c2c` on Linux reports cache lines that bounce between cores (JMH wraps it as `-prof perfc2c`). And a CPU profiler such as async-profiler, in lesson 6, shows the symptom: lots of samples on a trivial line such as `count++`.

There's also true sharing, which padding can't fix: many threads writing the same field, like an `AtomicLong` hit by every request. The only fixes there are to write less often or to split the value, which is what `LongAdder` does.
